q: Which principle means everyone is subject to the law?
e: The rule of law means the law applies to everyone.

q: Which action is an example of volunteering?
a: Helping at a community food bank without pay
e: Volunteers give their time freely to help others.

q: Which freedom allows people to follow a religion or have no religion?
e: Freedom of belief protects religious and non-religious beliefs.

q: What does tolerance mean in a diverse society?
e: Tolerance includes respecting people whose beliefs differ from yours.

q: Which is an example of taking part in local community life?
e: Community activities can bring neighbours together.

q: In which year did the Battle of Hastings take place?
e: The Norman conquest began with the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

q: Which document was agreed by King John in 1215?
e: Magna Carta was agreed in 1215 and is associated with limits on royal power.

q: Who was the first Tudor monarch?
e: Henry VII became king after the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485.

q: Which monarch ruled during the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588?
e: The Spanish Armada was defeated during the reign of Elizabeth I.

q: In which year did the Great Fire of London begin?
e: The Great Fire of London began in September 1666.

q: Which engineer is associated with the Great Western Railway?
e: Brunel designed major railway and engineering projects, including work on the Great Western Railway.

q: In which year did the First World War begin?
e: The First World War began in 1914.

q: In which year did the Second World War end in Europe?
e: Victory in Europe was celebrated in May 1945.

q: Who discovered penicillin?
e: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.

q: Which movement campaigned for votes for women?
e: Suffragists and suffragettes campaigned for women’s voting rights.

q: Which year is associated with the Act of Union between England and Scotland?
e: The Acts of Union took effect in 1707, creating the Kingdom of Great Britain.

q: Where does the UK Parliament meet?
e: The House of Commons and House of Lords meet at the Palace of Westminster.

q: What are the two Houses of the UK Parliament?
e: The UK Parliament has the House of Commons and the House of Lords.

q: What is the usual maximum period between UK general elections?
e: Under current law, a UK Parliament normally lasts no more than five years.

q: What does MP stand for?
e: An MP is a Member of Parliament.

q: Who normally leads the UK government?
a: The Speaker of the House of Commons
e: The Prime Minister heads the UK government.

q: Which institution interprets laws and resolves legal disputes?
e: Courts apply and interpret law in individual cases.

q: What is the voting age for UK parliamentary elections?
e: You must be at least 18 to vote in a UK parliamentary general election.

q: Which part of the UK has a devolved Parliament in Edinburgh?
e: The Scottish Parliament meets in Edinburgh.

q: Which devolved legislature meets in Cardiff?
e: Senedd Cymru, the Welsh Parliament, meets in Cardiff.

q: Where does the Northern Ireland Assembly meet?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Parliament Buildings, Stormont.

q: What is the capital of Scotland?
e: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.

q: What is the capital of Wales?
e: Cardiff is the capital of Wales.

q: What is the capital of Northern Ireland?
e: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

q: What is the capital of England?
e: London is the capital of England and of the UK.

q: Which is the highest mountain in the UK?
e: Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest mountain in the UK.

q: Which river runs through central London?
e: The River Thames flows through central London.

q: Which sea lies between Great Britain and Ireland?
e: The Irish Sea separates the islands of Great Britain and Ireland.

q: On what date is Christmas Day celebrated?
e: Christmas Day is celebrated on 25 December.

q: Which date is traditionally associated with Guy Fawkes Night?
e: Bonfire Night, or Guy Fawkes Night, is observed on 5 November.

q: Which flower is traditionally associated with England?
e: The rose is a traditional floral emblem of England.

q: Which plant is a traditional emblem of Scotland?
e: The thistle is a traditional emblem of Scotland.

q: Which saint is the patron saint of Wales?
e: St David is the patron saint of Wales.

q: Which saint is the patron saint of Northern Ireland?
e: St Patrick is associated with Ireland and Northern Ireland.

q: Which sport is played at Wimbledon?
e: Wimbledon hosts a famous annual tennis championship.

q: Who wrote the play Romeo and Juliet?
e: William Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet.

q: What is the name of the annual remembrance date on 11 November?
e: Armistice Day marks the 1918 armistice ending fighting in the First World War.

q: What are the two Houses of the UK Parliament?
e: The UK Parliament has the House of Commons and the House of Lords.

translations.ur: برطانوی پارلیمنٹ ہاؤس آف کامنز اور ہاؤس آف لارڈز پر مشتمل ہے۔
translations.hi: ब्रिटेन की संसद में हाउस ऑफ कॉमन्स और हाउस ऑफ लॉर्ड्स हैं।
translations.ar: يتكوّن البرلمان البريطاني من مجلس العموم ومجلس اللوردات.
translations.fr: Le Parlement britannique comprend la Chambre des communes et la Chambre des lords.

q: Which House of Parliament is directly elected by the public?
e: Members of the House of Commons are elected by voters.

translations.ur: ہاؤس آف کامنز کے ارکان کو ووٹر منتخب کرتے ہیں۔
translations.hi: हाउस ऑफ कॉमन्स के सदस्य मतदाताओं द्वारा चुने जाते हैं।
translations.ar: ينتخب الناخبون أعضاء مجلس العموم.
translations.fr: Les membres de la Chambre des communes sont élus par les électeurs.

q: What is the main role of an MP?
e: An MP represents people in a parliamentary constituency.

translations.ur: رکنِ پارلیمنٹ اپنے حلقے کے لوگوں کی نمائندگی کرتا ہے۔
translations.hi: सांसद संसद में अपने निर्वाचन क्षेत्र के लोगों का प्रतिनिधित्व करता है।
translations.ar: يمثل عضو البرلمان سكان دائرته الانتخابية.
translations.fr: Un député représente les habitants de sa circonscription.

q: Which institution interprets and applies the law in legal cases?
e: Courts decide cases by applying the law.

translations.ur: عدالتیں قانون نافذ کرکے مقدمات کا فیصلہ کرتی ہیں۔
translations.hi: अदालतें कानून लागू करके मामलों का फैसला करती हैं।
translations.ar: تفصل المحاكم في القضايا بتطبيق القانون.
translations.fr: Les tribunaux tranchent les affaires en appliquant la loi.

q: What is a referendum?
a: A public vote on a specific question
e: A referendum asks eligible voters to decide a particular issue.

translations.ur: ریفرنڈم میں اہل ووٹر کسی خاص مسئلے پر ووٹ دیتے ہیں۔
translations.hi: जनमत संग्रह में पात्र मतदाता किसी विशेष मुद्दे पर मतदान करते हैं।
translations.ar: الاستفتاء تصويت الناخبين المؤهلين على قضية محددة.
translations.fr: Un référendum permet aux électeurs de voter sur une question précise.

q: Which battle took place in 1066?
e: The Battle of Hastings took place in 1066.

translations.ur: ہیسٹنگز کی جنگ 1066 میں ہوئی تھی۔
translations.hi: हेस्टिंग्स का युद्ध 1066 में हुआ था।
translations.ar: وقعت معركة هاستينغز عام 1066.
translations.fr: La bataille d’Hastings a eu lieu en 1066.

q: Who signed the Magna Carta in 1215?
e: King John agreed to Magna Carta in 1215.

translations.ur: بادشاہ جان نے 1215 میں میگنا کارٹا سے اتفاق کیا۔
translations.hi: राजा जॉन ने 1215 में मैग्ना कार्टा स्वीकार किया।
translations.ar: وافق الملك جون على الماغنا كارتا عام 1215.
translations.fr: Le roi Jean a accepté la Magna Carta en 1215.

q: What was the name of the ship on which the Pilgrims sailed in 1620?
e: The Mayflower carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic in 1620.

translations.ur: مے فلاور 1620 میں زائرین کو بحرِ اوقیانوس کے پار لے گیا۔
translations.hi: मेफ्लावर 1620 में यात्रियों को अटलांटिक पार ले गया।
translations.ar: نقلت سفينة ماي فلاور الحجاج عبر الأطلسي عام 1620.
translations.fr: Le Mayflower a transporté les pèlerins à travers l’Atlantique en 1620.

q: In which year did the Great Fire of London start?
e: The Great Fire of London began in 1666.

translations.ur: لندن کی عظیم آگ 1666 میں شروع ہوئی۔
translations.hi: लंदन की भीषण आग 1666 में शुरू हुई।
translations.ar: بدأ حريق لندن الكبير عام 1666.
translations.fr: Le grand incendie de Londres a commencé en 1666.

q: Which queen ruled for much of the nineteenth century?
e: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901.

translations.ur: ملکہ وکٹوریہ نے 1837 سے 1901 تک حکومت کی۔
translations.hi: महारानी विक्टोरिया ने 1837 से 1901 तक शासन किया।
translations.ar: حكمت الملكة فيكتوريا من 1837 إلى 1901.
translations.fr: La reine Victoria a régné de 1837 à 1901.

q: What is the capital city of Wales?
e: Cardiff is the capital of Wales.

translations.ur: کارڈف ویلز کا دارالحکومت ہے۔
translations.hi: कार्डिफ़ वेल्स की राजधानी है।
translations.ar: كارديف عاصمة ويلز.
translations.fr: Cardiff est la capitale du pays de Galles.

q: What is the capital city of Scotland?
e: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.

translations.ur: ایڈنبرا اسکاٹ لینڈ کا دارالحکومت ہے۔
translations.hi: एडिनबरा स्कॉटलैंड की राजधानी है।
translations.ar: إدنبرة عاصمة اسكتلندا.
translations.fr: Édimbourg est la capitale de l’Écosse.

q: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
e: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

translations.ur: بیلفاسٹ شمالی آئرلینڈ کا دارالحکومت ہے۔
translations.hi: बेलफ़ास्ट उत्तरी आयरलैंड की राजधानी है।
translations.ar: بلفاست عاصمة أيرلندا الشمالية.
translations.fr: Belfast est la capitale de l’Irlande du Nord.

q: Which sea lies between Great Britain and Ireland?
e: The Irish Sea separates Great Britain from Ireland.

translations.ur: بحیرۂ آئرش برطانیہ اور آئرلینڈ کے درمیان ہے۔
translations.hi: आयरिश सागर ग्रेट ब्रिटेन और आयरलैंड के बीच है।
translations.ar: يفصل البحر الأيرلندي بريطانيا العظمى عن أيرلندا.
translations.fr: La mer d’Irlande sépare la Grande-Bretagne de l’Irlande.

q: Which of these is a country within the United Kingdom?
e: Wales is one of the four countries of the UK.

translations.ur: ویلز برطانیہ کے چار ممالک میں سے ایک ہے۔
translations.hi: वेल्स यूनाइटेड किंगडम के चार देशों में से एक है।
translations.ar: ويلز واحدة من الدول الأربع في المملكة المتحدة.
translations.fr: Le pays de Galles est l’une des quatre nations du Royaume-Uni.

q: Which flower is traditionally associated with England?
e: The rose is a traditional symbol of England.

translations.ur: گلاب انگلینڈ کی روایتی علامت ہے۔
translations.hi: गुलाब इंग्लैंड का पारंपरिक प्रतीक है।
translations.ar: الوردة رمز تقليدي لإنجلترا.
translations.fr: La rose est un symbole traditionnel de l’Angleterre.

q: Which plant is traditionally associated with Scotland?
e: The thistle is a traditional symbol of Scotland.

translations.ur: تھیسل اسکاٹ لینڈ کی روایتی علامت ہے۔
translations.hi: थिसल स्कॉटलैंड का पारंपरिक प्रतीक है।
translations.ar: الشوك رمز تقليدي لاسكتلندا.
translations.fr: Le chardon est un symbole traditionnel de l’Écosse.

q: On which date is Christmas Day celebrated in the UK?
e: Christmas Day is celebrated on 25 December.

translations.ur: کرسمس 25 دسمبر کو منایا جاتا ہے۔
translations.hi: क्रिसमस 25 दिसंबर को मनाया जाता है।
translations.ar: يُحتفل بعيد الميلاد في 25 ديسمبر.
translations.fr: Noël est célébré le 25 décembre.

q: Which sport uses a bat, ball and wickets?
e: Cricket is played with a bat, ball and wickets.

translations.ur: کرکٹ بلے، گیند اور وکٹوں سے کھیلی جاتی ہے۔
translations.hi: क्रिकेट बल्ले, गेंद और विकेट से खेला जाता है।
translations.ar: تُلعب الكريكيت بمضرب وكرة وويكيت.
translations.fr: Le cricket se joue avec une batte, une balle et des guichets.

q: Which action demonstrates respect for the law?
e: Respecting the law means following lawful rules and obligations.

translations.ur: قانون کا احترام کرنے کا مطلب قانونی قواعد کی پابندی کرنا ہے۔
translations.hi: कानून का सम्मान करने का अर्थ कानूनी नियमों का पालन करना है।
translations.ar: احترام القانون يعني الالتزام بالقواعد القانونية.
translations.fr: Respecter la loi signifie suivre les règles légales.

q: What does volunteering usually involve?
a: Giving time freely to help others
e: Volunteering means choosing to give time to help without expecting wages.

translations.ur: رضاکارانہ کام میں بغیر تنخواہ کے دوسروں کی مدد کے لیے وقت دیا جاتا ہے۔
translations.hi: स्वयंसेवा में बिना वेतन की अपेक्षा दूसरों की मदद के लिए समय दिया जाता है।
translations.ar: التطوع هو تقديم الوقت لمساعدة الآخرين دون انتظار أجر.
translations.fr: Le bénévolat consiste à donner du temps pour aider sans attendre de salaire.

q: Which of these best describes freedom of belief?
a: People may hold different religious or non-religious beliefs
e: Freedom of belief includes the right to have different religions or no religion.

translations.ur: عقیدے کی آزادی میں مختلف مذاہب یا کسی مذہب کو نہ ماننے کا حق شامل ہے۔
translations.hi: आस्था की स्वतंत्रता में अलग धर्म मानने या कोई धर्म न मानने का अधिकार शामिल है।
translations.ar: تشمل حرية المعتقد اعتناق أديان مختلفة أو عدم اعتناق دين.
translations.fr: La liberté de conviction comprend le droit d’avoir une religion ou aucune.

q: Which House has elected Members of Parliament (MPs)?
e: Elected MPs sit in the House of Commons.

translations.ur: منتخب اراکینِ پارلیمنٹ ہاؤس آف کامنز میں بیٹھتے ہیں۔
translations.hi: निर्वाचित सांसद हाउस ऑफ कॉमन्स में बैठते हैं।
translations.ar: يجلس النواب المنتخبون في مجلس العموم.
translations.fr: Les députés élus siègent à la Chambre des communes.

q: What is celebrated on 5 November in many parts of the UK?
e: Bonfire Night is traditionally marked on 5 November.

translations.ur: بون فائر نائٹ روایتی طور پر 5 نومبر کو منائی جاتی ہے۔
translations.hi: बॉनफायर नाइट परंपरागत रूप से 5 नवंबर को मनाई जाती है।
translations.ar: يُحتفل تقليديًا بليلة الألعاب النارية في 5 نوفمبر.
translations.fr: La nuit des feux de joie est traditionnellement célébrée le 5 novembre.

q: Which river flows through central London?
e: The River Thames flows through London.

translations.ur: دریائے ٹیمز لندن سے گزرتا ہے۔
translations.hi: टेम्स नदी लंदन से होकर बहती है।
translations.ar: يمر نهر التايمز عبر لندن.
translations.fr: La Tamise traverse Londres.

q: Which of these is a fundamental principle of British life?
e: Democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance and participation in community life are fundamental principles of British life.

q: Which of these is a responsibility of people living in the UK?
e: Everyone living in the UK is expected to respect and obey the law.

q: Which of these is a freedom that people in the UK enjoy?
a: Freedom to choose which laws to follow
e: Freedom of speech is one of the fundamental freedoms protected in the UK.

q: Which of these is a right that people in the UK have?
a: The right to avoid all taxes
The right to a fair trial
The right to choose their judge
The right to a free car
e: A fair trial is a basic legal right in the UK.

q: Which of these is a freedom offered to UK residents?
a: Freedom to vote more than once
Freedom to refuse to pay fines
e: UK law protects people from unfair discrimination.

q: What do new citizens say at a citizenship ceremony?
a: A promise to serve in the armed forces
An oath or affirmation of allegiance and a pledge
e: New citizens make an oath or affirmation of allegiance to the monarch and a pledge to respect the UK's rights, freedoms and laws.

q: To whom do new citizens swear or affirm allegiance at a citizenship ceremony?
a: The Speaker of the House of Commons
e: The oath or affirmation is made to the monarch, their heirs and successors.

q: What do you usually need to show to apply for settlement or citizenship?
a: Knowledge of English and of life in the UK
e: Applicants normally need to show they can speak and read English and have a good understanding of life in the UK.

q: Which statement about men and women in the UK is correct?
a: Men are paid more by law
They have equal rights to work and own property
e: Men and women have equal rights; it is illegal to discriminate at work on the grounds of sex.

q: What can a court issue to protect someone from being forced into marriage?
e: Courts can issue Forced Marriage Protection Orders; forcing someone to marry is a criminal offence.

q: Which statement about domestic violence in the UK is correct?
a: It is only illegal if a weapon is used
It is illegal, including between husband and wife
It is a private family matter
e: Domestic violence is a serious crime whoever commits it, including a husband against his wife or vice versa.

q: Which statement about female genital mutilation (FGM) is correct?
a: It is legal with parental consent
It is illegal in the UK
It is legal for adults only
It is legal if done abroad
e: FGM is illegal in the UK, and it is also a crime to arrange for it to be carried out abroad.

q: Is it legal to carry a weapon for self-defence in the UK?
a: Yes, if it is a knife under 30cm
No, carrying any weapon is a crime, even for self-defence
e: It is a crime to carry a weapon of any kind in public, even for self-defence.

q: Which of these is a way to take part in community life?
e: Volunteering is one of the most valued ways to contribute to your community.

q: If you are summoned for jury service, what must you do?
a: Ignore it if you are busy
Serve unless you have a valid reason to be excused
e: Anyone on the electoral register aged 18 to 75 can be asked to serve on a jury and must do so unless excused.

q: Who can volunteer to help run a local school as a governor?
a: Parents and other members of the local community
e: School governors are volunteers, often parents or local people, who help set the school's direction.

q: How can you register to donate blood?
a: Through the NHS Blood and Transplant service
e: In England you can register via NHS Blood and Transplant; each UK nation has its own service.

q: How can you help protect the environment in your area?
e: Recycling, saving energy and shopping locally all help the environment.

q: What is Neighbourhood Watch?
a: A scheme where neighbours help prevent crime in their area
e: Neighbourhood Watch schemes bring neighbours together to help prevent crime.

q: Which of these is illegal discrimination in the UK?
a: Refusing someone a job because of their race
Requiring a driving licence for a driving job
e: It is unlawful to discriminate because of protected characteristics such as race, sex, religion or disability.

q: Which body gives information about equality and human rights in England, Scotland and Wales?
a: The Equality and Human Rights Commission
e: The Equality and Human Rights Commission promotes equality and protects human rights.

q: Which Act brought the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law?
e: The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.

q: Which international agreement protecting human rights did British lawyers help draft after the Second World War?
a: The European Convention on Human Rights
e: British lawyers played a key role in drafting the European Convention on Human Rights.

q: Where is smoking banned in the UK?
a: In almost all enclosed public places
Nowhere; it is a personal choice
e: Smoking is banned in nearly all enclosed public places across the UK.

q: What is the minimum age to buy alcohol in the UK?
e: It is a crime to sell alcohol to anyone under 18, or to buy it for them.

q: What is the minimum age to buy tobacco products in the UK?
e: It is illegal to sell tobacco to anyone under 18.

q: What is the minimum age to enter a betting shop or casino?
e: You must be 18 to gamble in betting shops or casinos.

q: What must a dog wear in a public place?
a: A collar showing the owner's name and address
e: Dogs in public must wear a collar with the owner's name and address.

q: Which statement about cruelty to animals is correct?
a: It is allowed if the animal is yours
It is a civil matter only
It is a crime to treat a pet cruelly or neglect it
It is only illegal for farm animals
e: It is a criminal offence to treat a pet cruelly or to neglect it.

q: What should you do if you witness a crime?
a: Deal with it yourself using force
e: Reporting crime helps the police keep communities safe.

q: Which number should you call in an emergency in the UK?
e: 999 and 112 connect to emergency services; 101 is the non-emergency police number and 111 is the NHS non-urgent line.

q: Which number should you call to contact the police in a non-emergency?
e: 101 is the police non-emergency number.

q: Which of these statements about racial crime is correct?
a: Racial abuse is legal in private
Causing harassment because of someone's race is a crime
It is acceptable if meant as a joke
e: Racially motivated harassment and abuse are criminal offences.

q: What does it mean that the UK has a tradition of tolerance?
a: People respect others' right to hold different views
Everyone must share the same opinions
e: Tolerance means accepting and respecting different beliefs and lifestyles.

q: Which of these is a good way to help your community?
a: Helping elderly neighbours or volunteering locally
e: Helping neighbours and volunteering are encouraged ways to take part in community life.

q: When did Julius Caesar first lead a Roman invasion of Britain?
e: Julius Caesar led an unsuccessful invasion in 55 BC.

q: In which year did the Romans begin their successful invasion of Britain under Emperor Claudius?
e: The Roman conquest began in AD 43 under Emperor Claudius.

q: Who led a tribal revolt against the Romans?
e: Boudicca of the Iceni fought the Romans; her statue stands near the Houses of Parliament.

q: Which wall did the Romans build in the north of England?
e: Emperor Hadrian built the wall to keep out the Picts.

q: When did the Romans leave Britain?
e: The Romans left in AD 410 to defend other parts of their empire.

q: Where is Skara Brae, the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe?
e: Skara Brae is on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland.

q: Who won the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
e: William defeated King Harold and became William the Conqueror.

q: What does the Bayeux Tapestry commemorate?
a: The Norman conquest and the Battle of Hastings
e: The tapestry, now in France, tells the story of the Norman invasion.

q: What was the Domesday Book?
a: A record of towns, villages and landowners ordered by William the Conqueror
e: William ordered the Domesday Book to record who owned land in England.

q: Which king was forced to agree to Magna Carta in 1215?
e: Magna Carta limited the king's power and established that even the king was subject to law.

q: At which battle in 1314 did Robert the Bruce defeat the English?
e: Victory at Bannockburn kept Scotland unconquered by England.

q: Roughly what proportion of England's population died in the Black Death of 1348?
e: About one third of the population of England died.

q: Which king won the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
e: Henry V's victory at Agincourt is one of the most famous battles of the Hundred Years War.

q: Which two families fought the Wars of the Roses?
a: The Houses of Lancaster and York
e: Lancaster's symbol was a red rose and York's a white rose.

q: Which battle in 1485 ended the Wars of the Roses?
e: Henry Tudor won at Bosworth and became Henry VII, founding the Tudor dynasty.

q: Why did Henry VIII break away from the Church of Rome?
a: The Pope refused to grant him a divorce
e: Henry established the Church of England when the Pope would not annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon.

q: Who was Henry VIII's first wife?
e: Catherine of Aragon was a Spanish princess and Henry's first wife.

q: Who was the mother of Elizabeth I?
e: Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII's second wife, was Elizabeth I's mother.

q: In which year was the Spanish Armada defeated?
e: Elizabeth I's navy defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588.

q: When did the English Civil War begin?
e: War between Charles I and Parliament began in 1642.

q: Which king was executed in 1649?
e: Charles I was executed after the Civil War and England became a republic.

q: What title did Oliver Cromwell take after the Civil War?
e: Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector until his death in 1658.

q: When was the monarchy restored with Charles II?
e: The Restoration took place in 1660.

q: What was the Glorious Revolution of 1688?
a: The peaceful replacement of James II by William of Orange
The start of the Industrial Revolution
e: William of Orange took the throne with little bloodshed, hence 'Glorious'.

q: Which document of 1689 limited the power of the monarch and confirmed the rights of Parliament?
e: The Bill of Rights 1689 confirmed Parliament's rights and limits on royal power.

q: In which year did the Act of Union create the Kingdom of Great Britain?
e: The 1707 Act of Union joined England and Wales with Scotland.

q: In which year did Ireland become united with Great Britain?
e: Following the Act of Union of 1800, Ireland joined in 1801.

q: Who is generally regarded as the first Prime Minister?
e: Walpole was Prime Minister from 1721 to 1742.

q: Who led the Jacobite rebellion defeated at Culloden in 1746?
e: The Jacobites were defeated at the Battle of Culloden in 1746.

q: Which admiral won the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
e: Nelson died in the battle; Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square honours him.

q: Who defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
e: Wellington defeated Napoleon at Waterloo and later became Prime Minister.

q: In which year was the slave trade made illegal in British ships and ports?
e: The slave trade was abolished in 1807; slavery itself was abolished throughout the Empire in 1833.

q: Who was a leading campaigner for the abolition of slavery?
e: Wilberforce, an MP and evangelical Christian, campaigned against the slave trade.

q: Which engineer built the Great Western Railway?
e: Brunel built the Great Western Railway as well as bridges, tunnels and ships.

q: In which year did women over the age of 30 gain the right to vote?
e: Women over 30 could vote from 1918; equal voting at 21 came in 1928.

q: Which campaigner led the suffragette movement for women's votes?
e: Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union.

q: When did the First World War end?
e: The armistice took effect at 11am on 11 November 1918, remembered every year.

q: On which date did the D-Day landings take place?
e: Allied forces landed in Normandy on 6 June 1944.

q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
e: Fleming, a Scottish scientist, discovered penicillin.

q: Who was the first woman Prime Minister of the UK?
e: Margaret Thatcher served as Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990.

q: What type of constitution does the UK have?
a: A constitution written by the EU
An unwritten constitution not set out in a single document
e: The UK constitution is made up of laws, conventions and court judgments rather than one document.

q: What type of government system does the UK have?
a: A parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarch
e: The monarch is head of state but Parliament makes the laws.

q: Who is the UK's current head of state?
e: King Charles III became monarch in September 2022.

q: Which two houses make up Parliament?
a: The House of Commons and the House of Lords
e: Parliament consists of the elected Commons and the appointed Lords, along with the monarch.

q: How many parliamentary constituencies are there in the UK?
e: Each of the 650 constituencies elects one MP.

q: How often must a general election be held?
e: A general election must be held at least every five years.

q: Which voting system is used for general elections to the House of Commons?
e: The candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins.

q: Who is the head of the UK government?
e: The Prime Minister leads the government and appoints ministers.

q: What is the Prime Minister's official London residence?
e: The PM lives and works at 10 Downing Street.

q: What is the name of the Prime Minister's country house?
e: Chequers in Buckinghamshire is the PM's country residence.

q: Which minister is responsible for the economy?
e: The Chancellor manages the economy and public finances.

q: Which minister is responsible for crime, policing and immigration?
e: The Home Secretary oversees crime, policing and immigration.

q: Which minister manages the UK's relations with foreign countries?
e: The Foreign Secretary handles international relations.

q: What is the Cabinet?
a: A committee of senior ministers chosen by the Prime Minister
e: The Cabinet of around 20 senior ministers makes key government decisions.

q: Who usually becomes Leader of the Opposition?
a: A judge appointed by the King
The leader of the second-largest party in the Commons
e: The Leader of the Opposition leads the largest party not in government and appoints a shadow cabinet.

q: Who chairs debates in the House of Commons?
e: The Speaker is elected by MPs and remains politically neutral.

q: How do most members of the House of Lords get their seats?
a: They are chosen by local councils
e: Members of the Lords include life peers, some hereditary peers and Church of England bishops.

q: Which house of Parliament has the final say on new laws?
e: The Lords can suggest changes or delay laws, but the Commons is supreme.

q: Which statement about civil servants is correct?
a: They are elected by the public
They must belong to the governing party
e: Civil servants carry out government policy and must be politically neutral.

q: What does the government's 'whip' do?
a: Ensures discipline and attendance of party MPs in votes
e: Whips make sure MPs attend and vote with their party.

q: What happens when an MP dies or resigns?
a: The party with most seats takes it
The Prime Minister chooses a replacement
A by-election is held in their constituency
The seat stays empty until the next general election
e: A by-election elects a new MP for that constituency.

q: What is Hansard?
a: The official record of debates in Parliament
e: Hansard publishes what is said in Parliament.

q: Where does the Scottish Parliament sit?
e: The Scottish Parliament was formed in 1999 and sits at Holyrood in Edinburgh.

q: Where does the Welsh Parliament (Senedd) sit?
e: The Senedd, created in 1999 as the National Assembly for Wales, sits in Cardiff Bay.

q: Where does the Northern Ireland Assembly sit?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont in Belfast.

q: Which agreement in 1998 led to the creation of the Northern Ireland Assembly?
e: The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement led to power-sharing in Northern Ireland.

q: Which citizens can vote in UK general elections, if resident and old enough?
a: British, Irish and qualifying Commonwealth citizens
Only British citizens born in the UK
Any foreign national who pays tax
e: British, Irish and qualifying Commonwealth citizens resident in the UK can vote.

q: What must you do before you can vote?
e: You must be on the electoral register to vote in elections.

q: Which court deals with minor criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: Most minor criminal cases are dealt with in Magistrates' Courts; in Scotland it is the Justice of the Peace Court.

q: In England and Wales, which court hears serious criminal cases before a judge and jury?
e: Serious offences like murder are tried in the Crown Court.

q: How many people sit on a jury in Scotland?
e: Scottish juries have 15 members; juries in England, Wales and Northern Ireland have 12.

q: What age group is dealt with by Youth Courts?
e: Youth Courts hear cases involving people aged 10 to 17.

q: Up to what value can a small claim be made in England and Wales?
e: The small claims procedure handles disputes under £10,000 in England and Wales.

q: Which is an example of a civil law matter rather than a criminal one?
a: A dispute with a landlord about repairs
e: Civil law settles disputes between individuals or groups, such as housing and employment issues.

q: Who is the head of the Commonwealth?
e: The monarch is head of the Commonwealth, a voluntary association of countries.

q: Of which international body is the UK a permanent member of the Security Council?
e: The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

q: Which organisation collects income tax in the UK?
e: HMRC collects income tax and other taxes.

q: What do National Insurance contributions help to pay for?
a: State benefits, the State Pension and the NHS
e: National Insurance funds benefits and services including the State Pension and NHS.

q: In Great Britain, what is the minimum age to drive a car on public roads?
e: You can drive a car from 17 with a provisional licence in Great Britain.

q: In Great Britain, when must a car have an annual MOT test?
a: When it is more than three years old
Only if it has had an accident
From the day it is bought
e: Cars over three years old need a yearly MOT; in Northern Ireland the test applies from four years.

q: Which countries make up the United Kingdom?
a: England, Scotland, Wales and the Channel Islands
England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
e: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

q: Which countries make up Great Britain?
a: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
e: Great Britain refers to England, Scotland and Wales, not Northern Ireland.

q: Which statement about the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man is correct?
a: They are Crown dependencies, not part of the UK
They are part of the EU
e: They have their own governments and are not part of the UK.

q: What is the largest city in Scotland?
e: Glasgow is Scotland's largest city; Edinburgh is the capital.

q: Which crosses appear on the Union Flag?
a: The crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick
Only the cross of St George
The crosses of St Andrew and St David
The crosses of St George and St David only
e: The Union Flag combines the crosses of England, Scotland and Ireland.

q: Which country's emblem is not represented on the Union Flag?
e: Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was created.

q: What appears on the national flag of Wales?
e: The Welsh flag shows a red dragon on a white and green background.

q: Who is the patron saint of Scotland?
e: St Andrew is Scotland's patron saint.

q: Who is the patron saint of Wales?
e: St David is the patron saint of Wales.

q: Who is the patron saint of England?
e: St George is England's patron saint.

q: Who is the patron saint of Northern Ireland?
e: St Patrick is the patron saint of Northern Ireland.

q: Approximately how far is it from John O'Groats to Land's End?
e: It is around 870 miles (1,400 km) from the north of Scotland to the south-west of England.

q: What is Big Ben?
a: The great bell in the clock tower of the Houses of Parliament
e: Big Ben is the nickname of the bell; the tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

q: Where is the Eden Project?
e: The Eden Project in Cornwall has huge greenhouses housing plants from around the world.

q: Where is the Giant's Causeway?
a: On the north-east coast of Northern Ireland
e: Its hexagonal basalt columns were formed by volcanic activity millions of years ago.

q: Which national park includes the largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain?
e: Loch Lomond lies in Scotland's first national park.

q: Which is England's largest national park?
e: The Lake District in Cumbria is England's largest national park.

q: What is the largest natural lake in England?
e: Windermere is in the Lake District.

q: Which is the highest mountain in England?
e: Scafell Pike in the Lake District is England's highest peak.

q: Which is the highest mountain in Wales?
e: Snowdon is in Snowdonia (Eryri) National Park in north Wales.

q: Which was the first national park in the UK, designated in 1951?
e: The Peak District became the UK's first national park in 1951.

q: Which is the longest river in the UK?
e: The Severn flows from Wales into England; the Thames is the longest entirely in England.

q: Which river flows through London?
e: The Thames runs through the centre of London.

q: Which stretch of water separates England from France?
e: The Channel Tunnel runs beneath the English Channel.

q: Which country shares a land border with Northern Ireland?
e: Northern Ireland's only land border is with the Republic of Ireland.

q: In which city was the Titanic built?
e: The Titanic was built in Belfast's shipyards.

q: Where is the London Eye?
a: On the south bank of the River Thames
e: The observation wheel opened in 2000 on the South Bank.

q: Where is the Tower of London, home of the Crown Jewels?
e: The Tower was first built by William the Conqueror and is guarded by Yeoman Warders.

q: In which county is Stonehenge?
e: Stonehenge is a Stone Age monument in Wiltshire.

q: Where is the Principality (Millennium) Stadium?
e: The stadium in Cardiff hosts major rugby and football matches.

q: Which languages are spoken in parts of Scotland besides English?
e: Gaelic is spoken in parts of the Highlands and Islands.

q: Which language is widely spoken in Wales alongside English?
e: Welsh is taught in schools and widely spoken.

q: Which statement about Scottish and Northern Irish banknotes is correct?
a: They cannot be used in banks
They can only be used in their own country
They are valid across the UK, though shops do not have to accept them
e: The currency throughout the UK is the pound sterling.

q: On which side of the road do people drive in the UK?
e: Vehicles in the UK drive on the left.

q: Which national park is found in south Wales?
e: Bannau Brycheiniog, formerly known as the Brecon Beacons, is in south Wales.

q: On which date is Christmas Day celebrated?
e: Christmas Day celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ.

q: Which day after Christmas is a public holiday?
e: Boxing Day is 26 December and is a public holiday.

q: When is St David's Day?
e: St David's Day, Wales's national day, is 1 March.

q: When is St Patrick's Day?
e: St Patrick's Day is a public holiday in Northern Ireland.

q: When is St George's Day?
e: St George's Day is England's national day.

q: When is St Andrew's Day?
e: St Andrew's Day is Scotland's national day and a bank holiday there.

q: What do people commemorate on Bonfire Night, 5 November?
a: The end of the First World War
e: Guy Fawkes and others tried to blow up Parliament in 1605.

q: What do people wear to mark Remembrance Day?
e: Poppies remember those who died in war; Remembrance Day is 11 November.

q: What is Hogmanay?
e: Hogmanay celebrations are a major event in Scotland.

q: When is Halloween?
e: Halloween has ancient pagan roots; today children often go trick or treating.

q: Which day is April Fool's Day?
e: People play jokes on each other until midday on 1 April.

q: When is Mothering Sunday?
e: Mothering Sunday falls three weeks before Easter.

q: When is Father's Day celebrated in the UK?
e: Father's Day is the third Sunday in June.

q: What is another name for Shrove Tuesday?
e: Shrove Tuesday is the day before Lent begins.

q: Which festival is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs and is known as the festival of lights?
e: Diwali lasts five days and celebrates the victory of good over evil.

q: Which festival marks the end of Ramadan?
e: Eid al-Fitr celebrates the end of a month of fasting.

q: Which festival is celebrated by Jewish people for eight days?
e: Hanukkah, usually in November or December, remembers the Jews' struggle for religious freedom.

q: Which festival celebrates the founding of the Sikh community, the Khalsa?
e: Vaisakhi is celebrated on 14 April each year.

q: Which tennis tournament is the oldest in the world?
e: The Wimbledon Championships are held in London each summer.

q: Where is the home of golf?
e: Golf can be traced back to 15th-century Scotland.

q: Where is the Grand National horse race held?
e: The Grand National is one of the most famous horse races in the world.

q: Which two countries compete for the Ashes in cricket?
e: The Ashes is a historic Test series between England and Australia.

q: In which competition do England, Scotland, Wales, Ireland, France and Italy play rugby union?
e: The Six Nations is an annual rugby union tournament.

q: Where did the Paralympic Games originate?
e: Dr Sir Ludwig Guttmann organised sports for injured servicemen there.

q: In which years has London hosted the Olympic Games?
e: London has hosted the Olympic Games three times.

q: Who was the first person to run a mile in under four minutes?
e: Bannister achieved it in 1954.

q: Where was William Shakespeare born?
e: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in Warwickshire.

q: Who is known as Scotland's national poet?
e: Burns wrote 'Auld Lang Syne', sung at New Year.

q: Which author wrote 'Pride and Prejudice'?
e: Jane Austen's novels focus on marriage and family relationships.

q: Which author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
e: Conan Doyle was a Scottish doctor and writer.

q: What are the Proms?
a: An eight-week summer season of classical concerts
e: The Proms are held mainly at the Royal Albert Hall.

q: What is the Eisteddfod?
a: A Welsh festival of music, poetry and performance
e: The National Eisteddfod of Wales is one of the largest festivals of its kind in Europe.

q: What is the Turner Prize awarded for?
e: The Turner Prize is named after the painter J.M.W. Turner.

q: Which architect designed St Paul's Cathedral?
e: Wren rebuilt St Paul's after the Great Fire of London in 1666.

q: Who developed television in the 1920s?
e: Baird, a Scot, made the first television broadcasts.

q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
e: Berners-Lee created the web in 1990.

q: Who developed the jet engine?
e: Whittle, an RAF engineer, developed the jet engine in the 1930s.

q: What was Dolly the sheep, created in Scotland in 1996?
a: The first mammal cloned from an adult cell
The first animal sent into space
e: Dolly was cloned at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh.

q: Which food is traditionally associated with Scotland?
e: Haggis is a sheep's stomach stuffed with offal, suet, onions and oatmeal.

q: What is the UK's national anthem?
e: The anthem is sung at important national occasions.
